overview.title: The segmented banana and SAM's alternative masks
overview.subsection: 11.3.4 Prompting the model with a target point
overview.main_topic: Figure 11.12 shows the first candidate for the banana prompt; the text then plots the three remaining candidate masks (Figure 11.13) to show how they help with ambiguous prompts.
overview.central_idea: A single point is ambiguous; SAM's extra candidates represent alternative interpretations of the prompt (here: one banana vs. both bananas), and you can inspect them by indexing masks 1-3.
overview.importance: It shows why SAM returns four masks rather than one and how to access them, which is essential when the first mask is not the segmentation you wanted.
learning_objectives: Describe Figure 11.12 and relate it to the prompt (300, 550).
Use Python slicing (`[0][1:]`) to select the alternative candidates.
Build a 1 × 3 grid of subplots with Matplotlib and reuse the helpers on each axis.
Interpret Figure 11.13: which candidates cover one banana and which cover both.

summary:
The page opens with **Figure 11.12, "Segmented banana"**: the first candidate (index 0) for the prompt point (300, 550) covers the second banana from the left only, cleanly separated from the first banana even though their stems touch.

The text then asks about "the other mask candidates" and says they "can come in handy for ambiguous prompts". A listing plots the remaining three:

- `plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(20, 60))` creates one row of three axes;
- `masks = outputs["masks"][0][1:]` slices off the batch axis and keeps candidates 1, 2 and 3 (shape (3, 256, 256));
- in the loop, each axis gets the image, the prompt point and `get_mask(outputs, index=i + 1)` overlaid, titled `Mask 1`, `Mask 2`, `Mask 3`, with axes hidden.

**Figure 11.13** shows the result. In *Mask 1* the blue region again covers only the second banana. In *Mask 2* and *Mask 3* the region covers **both bananas**; the next page (p.351) states this explicitly: "an alternative segmentation found by the model includes both bananas."

The lesson: a click on one banana could legitimately mean "this banana" or "the bunch of bananas". SAM does not have to guess; it returns several plausible masks at different granularities, and it is up to the user (or to the `iou_pred` scores introduced on p.348) to pick the intended one.

paragraphs.excerpt: Now, what about the other mask candidates? Those can come in handy
paragraphs.what_it_says: The remaining three candidate masks are useful for ambiguous prompts; the listing plots them (Figure 11.13).
paragraphs.what_it_means: So far only candidate 0 was used. Candidates 1-3 are not noise; they are alternative answers to the same prompt. When a prompt could refer to several nested regions (part, object, group), different candidates capture different choices.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: In practice you often look at, or automatically score, all candidates instead of trusting the first. This is what makes a single-click interface workable for ambiguous cases.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: the SAM paper motivates multiple outputs with the 'whole, part, subpart' ambiguity of a single point, and trains the model so that only the best of the candidates is penalized for each training example, which encourages the candidates to diversify.

terminology.meaning: A prompt consistent with more than one reasonable segmentation, such as a point on one of two touching bananas.
One of the four masks SAM returns for a prompt.

connections: p.348: outputs["masks"] contains four 256 × 256 candidates and iou_pred their scores.
p.347: passing several labeled points (1 = include, 0 = exclude) is the book's other remedy for ambiguity.

concepts.name: Prompt ambiguity and multi-mask output
concepts.definition: A prompt can correspond to several valid segmentations; SAM addresses this by returning several candidate masks.
concepts.intuition: Pointing at one banana could mean that banana or the pair of bananas.
concepts.technical: Four masks (1, 4, 256, 256) plus predicted IoU per mask; index with [0][k].
concepts.significance: Lets an interactive user, or a program using iou_pred, pick the intended granularity.
concepts.example: Figure 11.13: Mask 1 covers one banana, Masks 2 and 3 cover both.
concepts.misconception: The alternative masks are not lower-quality versions of the same answer; they can be different, equally valid answers.

concepts.name: Point prompt
concepts.definition: Labeled (x, y) coordinates indicating the object to segment.
concepts.technical: Adding background points (label 0) is a way to disambiguate, as described on p.347.
concepts.misconception: A single point does not uniquely define an object.

concepts.name: Segment Anything Model (SAM)
concepts.definition: Promptable pretrained segmentation model used throughout 11.3.
concepts.intuition: A general 'select this' tool that offers several selections.
concepts.technical: Mask decoder emits several mask outputs per prompt.
concepts.misconception: SAM's first mask is not guaranteed to be the one you want.

code.title: Plotting the three alternative masks (Figure 11.13)
code.original_code:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(20, 60))
masks = outputs["masks"][0][1:]
for i, mask in enumerate(masks):
    show_image(image, axes[i])
    show_points(input_point, axes[i])
    mask = get_mask(outputs, index=i + 1)
    show_mask(mask, axes[i])
    axes[i].set_title(f"Mask {i + 1}", fontsize=16)
    axes[i].axis("off")
plt.show()
code.what_it_does: Creates a row of three plots and overlays candidate masks 1, 2 and 3 for the banana prompt on the image.

line_explanations.explanation: One row, three columns of axes; `axes` is an array of 3 Axes objects.
Drop the batch axis ([0]) and skip candidate 0 ([1:]) → shape (3, 256, 256).
Loop over the three remaining candidates; i = 0, 1, 2.
Draw the image and the prompt point on axis i.
Get candidate i + 1 (1, 2, 3) as a full-resolution boolean mask; this overwrites the loop variable.
Title each panel Mask 1/2/3 and hide tick marks.

code.inputs_outputs: Inputs: outputs from the banana prompt (p.349), image, input_point. Output: Figure 11.13.
code.algorithm: For k in 1..3: draw image, point, get_mask(k).
code.theory_link: Visual comparison of SAM's multi-mask output for an ambiguous prompt.
pitfalls: The loop variable `mask` from `enumerate(masks)` is unused: it is immediately replaced by get_mask's result. `for i in range(3):` would behave the same.
`figsize=(20, 60)` is much taller than needed for three square images in a row; Matplotlib keeps the images' aspect ratio, leaving blank space. Something like (20, 7) is more compact.
Using `index=i` instead of `i + 1` would re-plot candidate 0 and miss candidate 3.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written: show all four candidates with their predicted IoU in the title
scores = outputs["iou_pred"][0]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(24, 7))
for k in range(4):
    show_image(image, axes[k])
    show_points(input_point, axes[k])
    show_mask(get_mask(outputs, index=k), axes[k])
    axes[k].set_title(f"Mask {k}  iou_pred={float(scores[k]):.2f}")
    axes[k].axis("off")
plt.show()

deeper.title: Whole, part, or group?
deeper.body: Ask a friend to 'grab that' while pointing at one banana in a bunch: they may grab one banana or the whole bunch. Neither is wrong. SAM behaves like a polite friend who hands you both options and says how confident it is in each.

deeper.title: Two ways to resolve ambiguity
deeper.body: The book offers two tools: (1) look at the alternative candidates, as on this page; (2) add more labeled points (p.347), for example a background point (label 0) on the first banana to exclude it, or a second foreground point on it to include it. A third tool, a box prompt, comes on p.351: a box makes the spatial extent explicit.

questions.question: Which candidate indices does `outputs["masks"][0][1:]` contain?
questions.explanation: [0] removes the batch axis leaving 4 candidates; [1:] starts at index 1 and runs to the end. 0,1,2 would be [:3]; the others drop candidates.

questions.question: In Figure 11.13, which masks include both bananas?
questions.explanation: Mask 1 covers only the second banana, like Figure 11.12; the other two extend to the first banana (confirmed by the text on p.351).

questions.question: Why does it make sense for SAM to return several masks for one point?
questions.answer: A point does not specify the extent of the intended object; it may refer to a part, an object, or a group. Several candidates cover these interpretations.
questions.explanation: The banana prompt is the book's example: one banana or both are both plausible.

questions.question: What would happen if `index=i + 1` were changed to `index=i`?
options: Nothing; the same masks are plotted
Masks 0, 1, 2 would be plotted, so candidate 3 is never shown
questions.answer: Masks 0, 1, 2 would be plotted, so candidate 3 is never shown
questions.explanation: i runs 0-2. index=i selects candidates 0-2, all valid indices, so no error, but the titles would be off by one and candidate 3 skipped.

questions.question: Besides looking at alternative masks, how could you make SAM segment both bananas, or only one, more reliably?
questions.answer: Add more labeled points: a foreground point on the first banana to include it, or a background point (label 0) on it to exclude it. A box prompt (p.351) is another option.
questions.explanation: p.347 describes passing multiple labeled points to refine what is included and excluded.

questions.question: Can you explain why the loop variable `mask` from enumerate is never actually used?
questions.answer: Line 6 reassigns `mask` to get_mask(outputs, index=i + 1) before it is read, so only i matters.
questions.explanation: Recognising this helps you read and simplify example code.
